title: Ravenna — The Exile's End
teaser: In September, Dante Alighieri dies in Ravenna, having completed the greatest poem ever written in a language that barely existed as literature when he began. The Divine Comedy transforms Tuscan vernacular into the tongue of a nation — but the poet never sees Florence again.

art.label: Art
art.content: While Dante dies in Ravenna, in Florence Giotto di Bondone is painting the frescoes of the Bardi Chapel in Santa Croce — depicting the life of St. Francis with a naturalism that shatters Byzantine conventions. The same artist painted Dante's portrait in the Bargello Chapel, possibly from life. Giotto's revolution — volume, emotion, spatial depth — parallels Dante's literary breakthrough: both are turning from the hieratic to the human. The Proto-Renaissance is emerging in parallel channels: poetry that sounds like speech, painting that looks like seeing. Giotto's Francis grieves, doubts, bleeds. The art no longer points to heaven; it shows us earth as if heaven watches.
art.funFact: Dante mentions Giotto in Purgatorio XI, noting how the painter's fame has eclipsed his teacher Cimabue's — one of the earliest instances of an artist being named in vernacular literature.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: The Divine Comedy is complete — 14,233 lines of terza rima describing Dante's journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. It is the first major work of European literature written in vernacular rather than Latin, and its language — the Tuscan dialect — will become modern Italian. In De Vulgari Eloquentia, written in exile around 1304, Dante had argued that vernacular could achieve the dignity of Latin; the Commedia is the proof. The interlocking three-line rhyme scheme (ABA BCB CDC) drives the poem forward like nothing before it, each canto a self-contained universe within the larger cosmos. What Dante creates is simultaneously encyclopedic theology and raw autobiography — the summit of medieval vernacular literature.
lit.funFact: Florence repeatedly tried to recover Dante's bones after his death; Franciscan monks in Ravenna hid them for centuries, even bricking them into a wall during the Renaissance.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: The Commedia is often called 'the Summa in verse' — a poetic synthesis of Thomistic scholasticism. Dante places Thomas Aquinas in the Heaven of the Sun and structures Hell according to Aristotelian-Thomistic ethics: sins of incontinence, violence, and fraud arranged by increasing perversion of reason. Yet the poem is also a critique: the temporal Church appears corrupt, popes languish in Hell, and Dante's guide through Paradise is not a theologian but Beatrice, symbol of divine love apprehended through beauty. The Commedia simultaneously represents the apex of scholastic synthesis and its transcendence — reason illuminated by love, philosophy completed by poetry.
phil.funFact: Dante reserves the lowest circle of Hell — frozen in ice — for traitors, placing Brutus, Cassius, and Judas Iscariot in Satan's three mouths. Political betrayal equals theological betrayal.

hist.label: History
hist.content: Dante dies on September 14, 1321, returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice on behalf of his patron Guido II da Polenta. He has been in exile for nineteen years, condemned by the Black Guelphs who seized Florence in 1302 with papal backing. Across Europe, old orders are cracking: in Constantinople, the Byzantine civil war between two Andronikoi has begun; in France, lepers and Jews face massacres after well-poisoning accusations; in England, the barons revolt against Edward II. The Guelph-Ghibelline divide that defines Italian politics reflects a deeper fracture — the medieval synthesis of Church and Empire is dissolving into competing sovereignties.
hist.funFact: Dante's death sentence in Florence was finally revoked in 2008 — 706 years after his exile — by the city council, who declared it 'based on false charges.'

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The threads converge in Dante's exile itself. The same factional politics that drove him from Florence created the conditions for his masterpiece: the Commedia is shot through with bitter denunciations of Florentine corruption and yearning for a unified Italy under imperial justice. Giotto, still working in Florence, inhabits the world Dante was expelled from; both are transforming their arts by turning toward observed reality. The philosophical framework — Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotle and Christian theology — provides Dante's architecture, but the poem exists because politics shattered his life. The Franciscan order that sheltered Dante in Ravenna would, three years later, see William of Ockham summoned to Avignon for heresy — the nominalist philosophy that would crack scholasticism's foundations. Dante's poem arrives at the summit just as the descent begins.
